unit: Unit 3: Other Essential Elements of a Contract
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Capacity to Contract & Position of Minor
explain: Section 11 requires a person to be a major, of sound mind, and not disqualified by law to make a valid contract.
Under the Indian Majority Act 1875, every person domiciled in India attains majority at 18 years of age.
An agreement made by a minor is void ab-initio (Mohori Bibi vs. Dharmo Das Ghose 1903) and cannot be ratified upon turning major.
A minor can be a beneficiary or accept benefits under a contract, such as being admitted to partnership benefits (Section 30 Partnership Act).
Under Section 68, minor's estate is liable for necessaries supplied to him or his dependents, but the minor incurs no personal liability.

flow.title: Testing Minor Contract Enforceability
steps: Check age of contracting party
Identify if under 18 years
Agreement made is void ab-initio
Check if necessaries were supplied
Recover only from minor property

topics.example: Shruti, a minor, buys a study laptop for Rs. 70,000 on credit; the shopkeeper can recover up to Rs. 20,000 only from her assets and cannot hold her personally liable.
remember: No personal liability for minor; liability attaches only to property under Section 68.
mistakes: Assuming a minor becomes personally liable or can ratify a void agreement after attaining majority.

quiz.q: What is the legal status of an agreement entered into by a minor?
quiz.why: Under Indian Contract Act, any agreement with or by a minor is void from the very beginning.

quiz.q: Under Section 68, how can a supplier recover the cost of necessaries supplied to a minor?
o: Only from the minor's property or estate
quiz.why: The minor has no personal liability, but his estate is liable for necessaries supplied.

topics.title: Persons of Sound Mind & Disqualified Persons
explain: Section 12 defines a sound mind as the capacity to understand contract terms and form a rational judgment regarding its effect.
A person usually of unsound mind may contract during sane intervals when of sound mind.
A person usually of sound mind cannot contract while temporarily unsound, such as during delirium or severe drunkenness.
Contracts made by persons of unsound mind during unsoundness are void.
Other persons disqualified by law include foreign sovereigns, alien enemies, corporations, convicts, and insolvents.

flow.title: Determining Capacity based on Mental State
steps: Assess state of mind at contracting time
Determine capability of forming rational judgment
If sound at that moment contract valid
If unsound at that moment contract void

topics.example: A patient in a lunatic asylum who experiences lucid intervals of sound mind enters into a contract during such an interval; the contract is valid.
remember: Mental capacity is evaluated strictly at the exact time of making the contract.
mistakes: Assuming a person diagnosed with mental illness can never make a valid contract even during sane intervals.

quiz.q: A sane person who is severely drunk and incapable of understanding terms enters a contract. What is its status?
quiz.why: Under Section 12, a person cannot contract while delirium or drunkenness prevents rational judgment.

quiz.q: Which of the following persons is disqualified by law from entering into a contract?
quiz.why: Alien enemies fall under the specific legal status category of persons disqualified by law.

topics.title: Consent & Coercion
explain: Section 13 defines consent as two or more persons agreeing upon the same thing in the same sense (consensus ad idem).
Section 14 states consent is free when not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake.
Section 15 defines coercion as committing or threatening to commit an IPC-forbidden act, or unlawfully detaining property to force consent.
Threatening to commit suicide is recognized as coercion under Indian law.
Under Section 19, a contract induced by coercion is voidable at the option of the aggrieved party, and benefits must be restored under Section 72.

flow.title: Coercion Remedy Sequence
steps: Party commits or threatens forbidden act
Aggrieved party forced to give consent
Contract becomes voidable at victim option
Aggrieved party rescinds contract
Benefits received restored under Section 72

topics.example: A husband obtains a release deed from his wife under threat of committing suicide; the deed is voidable at the wife's option due to coercion.
remember: Coercion involves physical force or IPC forbidden acts.
Contracts caused by coercion are voidable under Section 19.
mistakes: Believing coercion must originate only from a contracting party, whereas it can proceed from a stranger.

quiz.q: Threatening to commit suicide to obtain consent for a contract is classified as:
quiz.why: Committing or threatening any act forbidden by the IPC is coercion under Section 15.

quiz.q: What is the effect of coercion on a contract under Section 19?
o: Voidable at the option of aggrieved party
quiz.why: Consent obtained by coercion renders the contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so obtained.

topics.title: Undue Influence
explain: Section 16 applies when relations enable one party to dominate the will of another to obtain an unfair advantage.
Dominance is deemed in real/apparent authority (master-servant), fiduciary relations (parent-child, solicitor-client, guru-devotee), or mental distress.
Unconscionable bargains with exorbitant terms create a legal presumption of undue influence against the dominant party.
The burden of proof lies on the dominant party to prove that consent was free once dominance and unfairness are shown.
Under Section 19A, the court may set aside such contracts completely or modify terms as just.

flow.title: Establishing Undue Influence
steps: Prove dominant relationship exists between parties
Show position used to gain unfair advantage
Presumption of undue influence arises
Dominant party must prove free consent
Court sets aside or modifies contract

topics.example: A money lender takes advantage of a poor farmer's financial distress to execute a bond at 6% monthly interest; the court can set aside or reduce the bond terms.
remember: Undue influence relies on moral or mental pressure between parties with a dominant relationship.
mistakes: Confusing high interest rates during general market scarcity with undue influence when no dominant relation exists.

quiz.q: Which relationship carries a presumption of fiduciary dominance under Section 16?
quiz.why: Fiduciary relationship of trust exists between a solicitor and client.

quiz.q: Under Section 19A, a contract induced by undue influence is:
o: Voidable at the option of aggrieved party
quiz.why: Undue influence renders the contract voidable at the option of the victim.

topics.title: Fraud
explain: Section 17 defines fraud as intentional deception, false assertions, active concealment, empty promises, or fraudulent acts.
Mere silence does not constitute fraud unless there is a duty to speak or silence is equivalent to speech.
The aggrieved party must rely on the false representation, be actually deceived, and suffer actual loss.
Remedies for fraud include rescinding the contract, suing for damages, or demanding performance putting the victim in the position as if true.
Exception: Silence amounting to fraud does not make contract voidable if victim had means of discovering truth with ordinary diligence.

flow.title: Fraud Action and Remedy Sequence
steps: False statement or active concealment made intentionally
Other party relies and gets deceived
Deceived party suffers actual monetary loss
Contract becomes voidable at victim option
Victim rescinds and sues for damages

topics.example: A seller actively conceals a major mechanical defect in a car to trick a buyer into purchasing it; the buyer can rescind and sue for damages.
remember: Remedies include both contract rescission AND damages.
mistakes: Assuming silence always constitutes fraud even when no duty to speak or equivalent speech exists.

quiz.q: Which remedy is available for fraud but NOT for innocent misrepresentation?
quiz.why: Damages can be claimed for fraud due to intentional deception, but not for innocent misrepresentation.

quiz.q: When does silence amount to fraud under Section 17?
o: When there is a legal duty to speak
quiz.why: Silence is fraud only when there is a duty to speak or when silence is equivalent to speech.

topics.title: Misrepresentation
explain: Section 18 defines misrepresentation as an innocent false statement of material fact made believing it to be true without intent to deceive.
It includes breach of duty without intent to deceive or innocently causing another party to make a mistake on subject matter.
The contract is voidable at the option of the aggrieved party under Section 19.
The victim can rescind the contract or demand performance, but CANNOT claim damages.
The right to rescind is lost if the aggrieved party affirms the contract or takes benefits after learning the truth.

flow.title: Misrepresentation Evaluation Process
steps: Party makes false statement believing it true
No intention to deceive exists
Other party enters contract relying on statement
Contract becomes voidable at victim option
Victim rescinds without claiming damages

topics.example: Sohan sells a motorcycle to Suraj stating it is in top condition based on second-hand belief; Suraj later agrees to let Sohan pay 40% repair costs, affirming the contract and losing rescission rights.
remember: No damages can be claimed for misrepresentation.
mistakes: Believing the aggrieved party can claim damages in cases of misrepresentation.

quiz.q: What is the key distinction between fraud and misrepresentation?
quiz.why: Fraud involves intentional deception, whereas misrepresentation is an innocent false statement.

quiz.q: If a party accepts partial repair benefits after discovering a misrepresentation, what is the outcome?
o: Loses the right to rescind contract
quiz.why: Taking a benefit or affirming the contract after knowing the truth waives the right to rescind.

topics.title: Mistake
explain: Mistake is an erroneous belief leading to misunderstanding between contracting parties.
Mistake of Indian Law (Section 21): Contract is NOT voidable because ignorance of law is no excuse.
Mistake of Foreign Law (Section 21): Treated as a mistake of fact; the agreement is void.
Bilateral Mistake of Fact (Section 20): Both parties are mistaken on an essential material fact; the agreement is void.
Unilateral Mistake of Fact (Section 22): Only one party is mistaken; contract remains valid (neither void nor voidable).

flow.title: Classifying Legal Effect of Mistake
steps: Identify type of mistake involved
If Indian law contract remains valid
If foreign law treat as fact mistake
If bilateral fact mistake contract is void
If unilateral fact mistake contract remains valid

topics.example: A and B contract to buy and sell a horse, but unknown to both, the horse was dead at the time of agreement; contract is void due to bilateral mistake.
mistakes: Assuming a unilateral mistake allows a party to void or rescind the contract.

quiz.q: What is the legal effect of a bilateral mistake on an essential fact under Section 20?
quiz.why: Where both parties are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to agreement, it is void.

quiz.q: How is a mistake regarding foreign law treated under the Indian Contract Act?
o: Mistake of fact making agreement void
quiz.why: Section 21 treats a mistake of foreign law as a mistake of fact, rendering the agreement void.

topics.title: Legality of Object and Consideration
explain: Section 23 states consideration or object is unlawful if forbidden by law, defeats legal provisions, is fraudulent, causes injury, is immoral, or opposed to public policy.
Agreements with unlawful object or consideration are void.
Under Section 24, if any part of a single consideration or object is unlawful and unseverable, the whole agreement is void.
If legal and illegal parts are severable, the court rejects the bad part and enforces the valid part.

flow.title: Testing Validity of Object and Consideration
steps: Examine object and consideration of agreement
Check if forbidden by law or fraudulent
Check if causing injury or immoral
If unlawful and unseverable agreement is void
If severable legal part is enforced

topics.example: A promises to pay B money if B prints a book violating another person's copyright; the agreement is void as the object causes injury to property and is forbidden by law.
remember: Unlawful consideration or object makes an agreement completely void.
mistakes: Assuming an illegal contract can be enforced if both parties mutually consent to it.

quiz.q: An agreement to commit a crime for money is void under Section 23 because:
quiz.why: Acts forbidden by law or punishable under statutes make the object unlawful and agreement void.

quiz.q: If an unlawful part of a consideration cannot be severed from the lawful part, what is the status of the agreement?
quiz.why: Under Section 24, if unlawful part cannot be severed, the entire agreement is void.

topics.title: Agreements Opposed to Public Policy
explain: Public policy restricts contract freedom to protect community welfare.
Agreements opposed to public policy are void under Section 23.

Examples: Trading with an alien enemy, stifling prosecution of non-compoundable offences, maintenance and champerty (if malicious/unreasonable), trafficking in public offices/titles, creating monopolies, marriage brokerage, and interfering with justice.
Compoundable criminal offences can be lawfully compromised without violating public policy.

flow.title: Evaluating Public Policy Violations
steps: Identify nature of agreement
Check against recognized public policy heads
Determine if harming public interest
If opposed to public policy declare void
No legal action allowed to recover money

topics.example: Harish pays Rs. 15,000 to an officer to procure a government job for his son; when the officer fails, Harish cannot recover the money as it is trafficking in public office.
remember: Public policy agreements are void; money paid under them cannot be recovered.
mistakes: Believing marriage bureaus are illegal marriage brokerage contracts (bureaus only provide information without negotiating marriage for reward).

quiz.q: An agreement to pay money to a public official to procure a government job is void because it is:
quiz.why: Trading or paying money for public appointments interferes with public service and is opposed to public policy.

quiz.q: Maintenance and champerty agreements in India are valid UNLESS:
o: They are unreasonable, unjust, or maliciously motivated
quiz.why: Supplying funds for litigation is valid in India unless unreasonable or maliciously motivated for gambling in litigation.

topics.title: Expressly Declared Void Agreements
explain: Section 26: Agreements in restraint of marriage of any person (other than a minor) are void.
Section 27: Agreements in restraint of trade are void, except sale of goodwill or reasonable partner restrictions (Partnership Act).
Section 28: Agreements in restraint of legal proceedings are void, except valid arbitration agreements.
Section 29: Agreements with uncertain or ambiguous meaning are void unless capable of being made certain.
Section 56: Agreements to perform impossible acts are void.

flow.title: Assessing Expressly Declared Void Contracts
steps: Check if restricting marriage trade or remedies
Check if terms are uncertain or impossible
Look for statutory exceptions like goodwill sale
If no exception applies declare void

topics.example: A agrees to sell B '100 tons of oil' without specifying the type, and A deals in many kinds of oil; the agreement is void for uncertainty under Section 29.
remember: Restraints on marriage, trade, and legal proceedings are void by default, subject to narrow statutory exceptions.
mistakes: Thinking a service agreement restraining an employee from competing during employment is void (it is valid).

quiz.q: An agreement restraining a major person from marrying is:
quiz.why: Every agreement in restraint of marriage of any person other than a minor is void.

quiz.q: Which of the following trade restraints is VALID by way of exception?
o: Preventing a seller of goodwill from trading anywhere in India forever
Restraining an outgoing partner from carrying on similar business within reasonable local limits
Total ban on an employee from working anywhere after resignation
Agreement among all sellers to eliminate competition completely
quiz.why: Section 36 of Partnership Act allows reasonable local limits restraint on outgoing partners.

topics.title: Wagering Agreements & Insurance Contracts
explain: Section 30: Wagering agreements are promises to pay money upon the outcome of an uncertain event where neither party has control or other interest.
Wagers are void, and no suit can be filed to recover winnings.
Speculative transactions, lotteries, and horse race bets under Rs. 500 are wagering and void.
Exceptions (NOT wagers): Chit funds, commercial stock delivery contracts, skill games/athletic contests (prize <= Rs. 1,000), horse races (prize >= Rs. 500), and insurance contracts.
Insurance vs Wager: Insurance requires insurable interest, mutual consideration, indemnifies loss, and is enforceable; wagers lack insurable interest and consideration, and are void.

flow.title: Determining Wagering vs Valid Contingent Contracts
steps: Identify contract subject matter
Check if parties have insurable interest
Check if outcome depends purely on chance
If pure betting declare void wager
If valid insurance enforce contract

topics.example: A and B bet Rs. 50,000 on whether it will rain today; this is a wagering agreement and is void under Section 30.
remember: Wagers require mutual chance of gain/loss and no insurable interest.
Insurance contracts are valid and enforceable.
mistakes: Confusing valid insurance contracts with void wagering agreements.

quiz.q: What is the legal status of a wagering agreement under Section 30?
quiz.why: Section 30 expressly declares agreements by way of wager to be void.

quiz.q: A contract of insurance differs from a wager because an insurance contract requires:
quiz.why: Insurance contracts require insurable interest in life/property and premium consideration, making them valid.
